topicTitle: Introduction: Three domains of life, binomial nomenclature, five kingdom classification system (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia)
notes: **Three domains (Woese, 1990):** Archaea (primitive prokaryotes, extremophiles), Bacteria (true bacteria), Eukarya (eukaryotes). Based on rRNA sequencing.
**Binomial nomenclature (Linnaeus, 1753):** each species has a two-part scientific name: Genus + species. Italicised, Genus capitalised, species lowercase. Example: Homo sapiens.

**Five kingdoms (Whittaker, 1969):** Monera (prokaryotes), Protista (unicellular eukaryotes), Fungi (heterotrophic absorbers), Plantae (autotrophic multicellular), Animalia (heterotrophic multicellular). Basis: cell structure, nutrition, body organisation, phylogeny.

**Kingdom Monera:** prokaryotic cells (no true nucleus), peptidoglycan cell wall (in bacteria), single circular DNA, no membrane-bound organelles. Includes archaebacteria (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles) and eubacteria (cyanobacteria, mycoplasma).

**Kingdom Protista:** unicellular eukaryotes, mostly aquatic, includes photosynthetic (euglenoids, diatoms, dinoflagellates) and heterotrophic forms (protozoans like Amoeba, Paramecium). Cell wall may be present or absent; nutrition is variable.

**Kingdom Fungi:** eukaryotic, heterotrophic (absorptive nutrition), cell wall of chitin and polysaccharides, body is a mycelium of hyphae. Saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic. Examples: yeasts, moulds, mushrooms.

**Kingdom Plantae:** multicellular, eukaryotic, autotrophic (photosynthetic), cell wall of cellulose, store food as starch. Range from simple algae (in some classifications) to angiosperms with complex vascular tissue.

**Kingdom Animalia:** multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic (holozoic nutrition), no cell wall, store food as glycogen. Most show locomotion, sexual reproduction, and embryonic development with blastula stage.

**Archaea vs Bacteria:** both are prokaryotes but differ in rRNA sequence, cell wall composition (archaea lack peptidoglycan, have pseudomurein), membrane lipids (archaea have branched isoprenoid ethers), and habitat (archaea thrive in extreme conditions).

**Why two kingdom systems are inadequate:** Aristotle's plants vs animals failed for organisms like Euglena (photosynthetic + motile), fungi (non-photosynthetic, non-motile, not animal), and bacteria (prokaryotic, neither).
**Taxonomic hierarchy (in order):** Kingdom > Phylum (Division for plants) > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species. Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

**ICBN and ICZN rules:** International Code of Botanical Nomenclature governs plant names; International Code of Zoological Nomenclature governs animal names. Both mandate Latin or Latinised names, valid publication, and priority of the earliest valid name.

**Concept of species:** a group of closely related organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring. A species is reproductively isolated from others (biological species concept by Ernst Mayr).

**Three principles of binomial nomenclature:** (1) generic name + specific epithet, (2) Latin language, (3) author's name abbreviated at the end (e.g., Homo sapiens Linn.). Triticum aestivum Linn. is the scientific name of wheat.

**Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic cell:** prokaryotes lack membrane-bound nucleus and organelles, are usually 1-10 micrometres, and have circular DNA. Eukaryotes have a true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, are 10-100 micrometres, and have linear chromosomes.
confusion: Do not confuse this concept with similar-sounding terms. Check definitions carefully.
Always verify the conditions under which the formula applies — many formulas have restricted domains.
Sign conventions matter. Define your coordinate system before applying equations.
Archaea and Bacteria are BOTH prokaryotes — Archaea are NOT the same as Eukarya. Domain 'Archaea' is distinct from 'Bacteria' despite both being prokaryotic.
Binomial nomenclature uses the Genus name capitalised and species epithet in lowercase — both are italicised, but never capitalise the species epithet (e.g., Mangifera indica, not Mangifera Indica).

The five-kingdom system is not the same as the three-domain system. Three-domain is a higher rank; five-kingdom fits within the Eukarya domain (plus Monera is split into Archaea and Bacteria in three-domain).
Whittaker's system classifies Fungi as a separate kingdom from plants — fungi are NOT plants, despite being historically grouped with them.
Protista is a 'catch-all' kingdom and is considered paraphyletic (not a true clade); some modern classifications are moving away from it.

**Q1:** Write the scientific name of mango following binomial nomenclature. *Ans:* Mangifera indica Linn. (Genus capitalised, species in lowercase, both italicised, author abbreviation at the end).

**Q2:** Who proposed the three-domain system and what was the basis of classification? *Ans:* Carl Woese (1990) proposed the three-domain system based on differences in 16S rRNA nucleotide sequences. The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

**Q3:** Differentiate between Archaea and Bacteria. *Ans:* Archaea lack peptidoglycan in their cell wall, have ether-linked branched lipids in membranes, and live in extreme environments. Bacteria have peptidoglycan cell walls, ester-linked straight lipids, and live in moderate environments. Both are prokaryotes.

**Q4:** Why was the two-kingdom classification (Plantae and Animalia) considered inadequate? *Ans:* It failed to classify organisms like Euglena (both photosynthetic and motile), fungi (heterotrophic, non-motile, with cell wall), and bacteria (prokaryotic, no clear plant/animal features).

**Q5:** List the five kingdoms of Whittaker and the main criterion used to classify them. *Ans:* Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Criteria: cell structure (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular/multicellular), nutrition mode (autotrophic/heterotrophic), and phylogenetic relationships.

The first scientific name accepted under binomial nomenclature was that of the wild briar rose, Rosa canina, by Linnaeus in his Species Plantarum (1753).
Carl Woese discovered archaea as a separate domain in 1977 by comparing 16S ribosomal RNA sequences — this overturned the long-held belief that life had only two major divisions.
Modern estimates suggest Earth hosts around 8.7 million eukaryotic species, of which only ~1.5 million have been formally described and named.
The 'Father of Taxonomy' is Carl Linnaeus (1707-1778), who published Systema Naturae (1735) and Species Plantarum (1753), the starting point for binomial nomenclature.
R.H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom system in 1969, replacing the older two-kingdom (Linnaeus) and three-kingdom (Haeckel) classifications.
